en: Itivuttaka 111 Catukkanipāta Brāhmaṇadhammayāgavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One, spoken by the Sublime One, so I have heard: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of offerings. What four? The offering of material things, the offering of Dhamma, the offering of fearlessness, and the offering of loving-kindness. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of offerings. So it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Fortunate One further said this: “The offering of material things, the offering of Dhamma, The offering of fearlessness, and the offering of loving-kindness— These four offerings, when practiced well, Lead to the attainment of heaven. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus was it said by the Blessed One, so I have heard. In this connection, the Blessed One spoke these verses: “The offering of material things, the offering of Dhamma, The offering of fearlessness, and the offering of loving-kindness— These four offerings, when practiced well, Lead to the attainment of heaven. The Discourse on Perfect Virtue.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:

“Monks, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; undertake and train yourselves in the rules of training.”
“Bhikkhus, for you who dwell with virtue perfected, with the Pātimokkha perfected, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,
perfect in conduct and resort, seeing fear in even the slightest faults, and training yourselves by undertaking the rules of training—
what further task remains to be done?”
But even when walking, monks, if a bhikkhu’s covetousness has vanished, his ill will has vanished, his sloth and torpor have vanished,
his restlessness and remorse have vanished, his doubt has been abandoned, his energy is aroused and unflagging,
his mindfulness is established and unconfused, his body is tranquil and unaroused, and his mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
“Cāraṃpi, bhikkhave, a bhikkhu who has become thus is called ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.
And if, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is standing, covetousness and ill will have vanished from him … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … and doubt have been abandoned;
if his energy is aroused and unflagging, and mindfulness is established...”
He is mindful and clearly comprehending; his body is tranquil and unagitated; his mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
Monks, even when standing, a monk who has become thus is called "ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.
And when sitting, monks, if a monk’s covetousness and ill will have vanished... [and] sloth and torpor...
… restlessness and remorse … doubt have been abandoned; energy is aroused and not slackened;
mindfulness is established and unconfused; the body is tranquil and not agitated; the mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
Monks, a monk who is thus seated, being ardent, ashamed [of evil], constantly and continuously energetic and resolute, is called such.
“Monks, even when a bhikkhu is lying down and awake, if his covetousness and ill will have vanished;
… if his sloth and torpor … his restlessness and remorse … his doubt have been abandoned; if his energy is aroused and unflagging;
if his mindfulness is established and unmuddled; if his body is tranquil and unagitated; and if his mind is concentrated and one-pointed—[then he is said to be practicing rightly].”
“Monks, even while lying down, a monk who is thus awake, ardent, and ashamed [of evil], constantly and continuously energetic and resolute, is said to be ‘one who has exerted himself.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Restrained he should walk, restrained he should stand,
restrained he should sit, restrained he should lie down;
restrained the bhikkhu should bend and stretch his limbs.”
One should extend it with effort—
upward, across, and downward,
as far as the reach of the world extends.
And having contemplated the arising and passing away of the aggregates of phenomena,
one who dwells thus with inward composure—
Tranquil in conduct, not agitated,
always mindful, training in the proper way of mental serenity.
"One who is constantly resolute—such a one they call a bhikkhu," so it was said.
This matter, too, was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The twelfth.
